case_name: Durham Children’s Aid Society v. F.H.
text:
Whitby
COURT
FILE NO.:
FC-06-163

ONTARIO

SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE

B E T W E E N:

)

)

DURHAM

CHILDREN’S AID SOCIETY

)

)

)

Matthew Price, for the Applicant

)

Applicant

F. H. and R. B.

for the Respondent F.H.; Bobbette Jones-Keita, for the Respondent R.B.

)

Respondents

HEARD:
May
11-15; June 2, 16, 19; July 28 & 29, 2009

REASONS
FOR JUDGMENT

INGRAM J.

[
1
]

In this proceeding the Durham Children’s Aid
Society (“CAS”) seek:

(a)

an order of Crown wardship with no access to the
parents for Alizeah Victoria B., born December 28, 2004, and for Anthony
Richard B., born January 11, 2006; and

(b)

a finding that Richard Junior Shakur B., born
November 10, 2007, is a child in need of protection and an order for Crown
wardship with no access to the parents.

[
2
]

The parents of the children, F.H., age 22, and
R.B., age 26, seek the return of the children to parental care.

[
3
]

These children were apprehended in Durham
Region. They have no religious affiliation.

[
4
]

Alizeah and Anthony reside together in the same
foster home and have been in the care of the CAS since July 13, 2006. Richard
Junior is in a different foster home and has been in the care of the CAS since
December 23, 2007. Each of these children has been in care beyond the statutory
guidelines set out in
s. 70
of the
Child and Family Services Act
, R.S.O.
1990, c. C.11 (
CFSA
) such that the only option for the court in this
case is to return the children to their parents or make an order for Crown
wardship.  Section 70 of the
CFSA
states the following:

70 (1)   Subject to subsections (3) and (4), the
court shall not make an order for society wardship under this Part that results
in a child being a society ward for a period exceeding,

(a)  12 months, if the child is less than 6 years of age on the day
the court makes an order for society wardship; or

(b)  24 months, if the child is 6 years of age or older on the day
the court makes an order for society wardship.

(2)  In calculating
the period referred to in subsection (1), time during which a child has been in
a society’s care and custody under,

(b)  a
temporary order made under clause 51(2)(d), shall be counted.

BACKGROUND

Pre-Apprehension and Apprehension

[
5
]

This family came to the attention of the Durham
CAS in May 2006 after the mother of the children, F.H., was hospitalized after
being the victim in a hit and run motor vehicle accident. Attempts by the CAS
to contact the family were not successful until June 22, 2006, when Ms. F.H.
contacted the CAS to set up an appointment for the following Monday. She later
postponed the meeting.

[
6
]

On July 5, 2006, CAS worker Jodie Barber spoke
with R.B., who related that he and F.H. had had an argument over suspicions
that he was “cheating” on her, which he denied.  F.H. took the children to her
mother’s residence.  R.B. later attended at this residence and found that the
children were unkempt, had wet diapers, inappropriate bedding, no formula and
were going to be left in the care of a young babysitter while F.H. went to a
nightclub. There was no food available for the children. The police were called
and R.B. eventually left with the children.

[
7
]

On July 6, 2006, Jodie Barber of the CAS
requested that the parents go to the Oshawa Clinic for drug screening. This
issue of drug screening remains an issue today, some three years after the
original request, despite repeated requests both verbally and in writing by the
CAS and by court order. R.B. took one test that was positive for cocaine. He
disputed the results but has not provided the results of any subsequent tests
to the CAS.

[
8
]

R.B. commenced domestic proceedings on July 6,
2006 to obtain a custody order. On the same day F.H. reported to the CAS that
R.B. was physically, verbally and emotionally abusive to her and she had been
in hiding. She agreed to complete drug testing.

[
9
]

On July 13, 2006 the father took Anthony to be
examined by Dr. Rajah, as directed by the CAS. Due to the child’s abnormal head
circumference, Anthony was referred for further testing at the Hospital for
Sick Children where he was admitted until July 19, 2006. The medical report of Dr.
Marcellina Mian from the Hospital for Sick Children, filed as Exhibit 1, is
inconclusive as to the cause of the head size:

His MRI and clinical pictures are perplexing as
to the contribution of congenital abnormalities and trauma in the development
of his subdural haemorrhages and optic nerve atrophy. Essentially his findings
could be due to one or the other or both, which leads to a real dilemma in
planning for this child’s safety and well-being. If his problem is congenital
then there is no reason for Anthony and his sister to need society’s
protection. However, if the problem is trauma, then his safety and well being
and potentially that of his sister are in jeopardy in the environment in which
they found themselves prior to coming to medical attention.

[
10
]

At the initial return of the Protection Application, F.H. spoke to
Jodie Barber privately and related that R.B. had physically abused her
throughout their relationship.  R.B. and F.H. reconciled the same day.

[
11
]

The CAS sought to keep the children in their temporary care due to the
reports of domestic violence, including the mother’s acknowledgement of this violence;
the failure of the parents to complete drug testing; and the inconclusive
findings of the physicians at the Hospital for Sick Children.

Post-Apprehension to Trial

[
12
]

It took almost three years for this case to reach trial. The parties
separated and reconciled many times. The police were called several times by
mother, father, the CAS and neighbours. Promises were given by the parents that
included completion of counselling, attendance at school, participating in drug
testing, and finding stable housing. With the exception of the mother finding employment
with a fast food chain, most of these promises were never fulfilled. There were
several documented incidents of the parties being together despite warnings
from police and CAS workers that they were in breach of the court orders. A few
incidents will be related in the chronology of this case.

[
13
]

Although both parents attended court on July 17, 2006 when the case
was adjourned to September 1, 2006, neither parent returned to the court on
September 1, 2006. Having failed to file material and having failed to attend
court, they were noted in default.

[
14
]

In mid-September 2006, following yet another dispute with F.H., R.B.
was arrested and detained.  In her statement to Officer Richardson of the
Durham Regional Police, which she verified at trial, F.H. indicated that R.B.
had stripped her such that she would be unable to leave the apartment. He
followed her from room to room, occasionally punching her and pricking her with
a steak knife. He placed a condom over a steak knife and inserted it into her
vagina. He poured candle wax down her back. He grabbed her neck and threatened
to slit her throat.

[
15
]

Although R.B. denied these allegations, he was placed in custody on
September 12, 2006. The following day he gave a statement to Officer Richardson
alleging that mother had a drug problem, using crack, ecstasy and alcohol
regularly. A large quantity of ecstasy was found in the apartment. He indicated
that she had remained in the bathroom the previous evening because she knows
that his family, who were visiting, did not like her. He also mentioned that
they used public washrooms, as there was no hydro or hot water in their
apartment, not appropriate conditions for children.  He was released on
December 6, 2006.

[
16
]

While R.B. was in custody, F.H. missed several of her access visits
such that her visits at the Access Centre were cancelled. She was encouraged by
the victim witness personnel to relocate to Hamilton, but did not do so. She was encouraged to take drug testing, but
failed to do so.

[
17
]

Upon motion for summary judgment brought by the CAS, an order was
made on November 20, 2006 finding the two children in need of protection
pursuant to sections 37(2)(a)(i), 37(2)(b)(i), 37(2)(b)(ii) and 37(2)(g) of the

CFSA
and the children were made wards for a period of six months.

37 (2)  A child is in need of protection where,

(a)
the child has suffered physical harm, inflicted by the person having

charge
of the child or caused by or resulting from that person’s,

(i)
failure to adequately care for, provide for, supervise or protect the child, or

….

(b)
there is a risk that the child is likely to suffer physical harm inflicted by
the person having charge of the child or caused by or resulting from that
person’s,

….

(ii)
pattern of neglect in caring for, providing for, supervising

or
protecting the child.

….

(g)
there is a risk that the child is likely to suffer emotional harm of the kind
described in subclause (f) (i), (ii), (iii), (iv) or (v) resulting from the
actions, failure to act or pattern of neglect on the part of the child’s parent
or the person having charge of the child;

[
18
]

In her endorsement, Madam Justice Eberhard wrote the following:
“worker indicates that services have been, will continue to be offered to
mother but to date mother has not followed through”.

[
19
]

The CAS outlined their expectations for the parents in the Plan of
Care that was filed at the time the children were found in need of protection.
These included the following:

(a)

attend counselling concerning domestic violence,

(b)

attend for random drug testing,

(c)

notify the CAS prior to any changes of address
or phone number,

(d)

sign releases of information,

(e)

attend a parenting course.

Completion of
these tasks does not appear to have been a priority for either parent.

[
20
]

R.B. was released from custody on December 6, 2006 upon terms, one
of which was to have no contact with F.H.  He indicated to Monifa St. Hill, the
primary CAS caseworker, that the parents intended to resume their relationship.
She gave the parents a copy of the Plan of Care and a letter indicating CAS
expectations that the parents would attend a parenting course and that R.B. attend
a Partner Assault Response Service (“PARS”) program designed for men who abuse
their partners.

[
21
]

During the early part of 2007, despite the fact that the parents
were not to see one another, there were several reported instances of breaches
of this condition.

[
22
]

In the Status Review Application brought in May 2007, the CAS sought
an order for Crown wardship with no access, for the purposes of adoption. At
the time that the Status Review Application was commenced, unknown to the CAS
staff, F.H. was pregnant with her third child, the father being R.B.

[
23
]

Both parents filed Answers and Plans of Care. In her Answer of June
1, 2007, F.H. reiterates the fact that she has been physically and emotionally
abused by R.B. Her plan was to live with her mother, sister and children in a
new residence that would be obtained by her mother. She was planning to enrol
in counselling and even indicated the time of her first appointment. She failed
to carry through.

[
24
]

She states in her Plan of Care, “I no longer have a relationship
with the co-respondent, nor will I have one in the future.” Her plans changed
quickly as two months later she received $80,000 from an accident settlement and
proceeded to buy R.B., the one she accused of frequently abusing her,  a car
for $14,000. She used some of the proceeds to buy expensive jewellery and gifts
for family members, yet she testified that she and R.B. could not carry on with
counselling due to fees totalling $840 (twelve sessions at $70 each). It
appears that acquiring personal items for themselves was more important than
working towards the return of their children.

[
25
]

R.B., in his Answer and Plan of Care dated May 10, 2007, indicated that
he would live with the children and his mother in their present four bedroom
house. He would be returning to school in September 2007. He states that F.H.
is an “immature, and irresponsible parent and she is not capable of providing
for the children.” He sought an order that F.H.’s access to the children be
supervised at an Access Centre. He acknowledged that his relationship with F.H.
had been a tumultuous one.

[
26
]

Several court attendances took place while waiting for the parents
to find counsel and file material. A trial management conference was set for
September 10, 2007, but that did not take place. It would take twenty months
for this case to reach trial.

[
27
]

The parents were informed that family members could put forward
plans for the children. A Kinship Assessment was started, involving members of
both families. The case was adjourned, despite the fact that the children had
been in care for more than the statutory limit contemplated in the
CFSA
,
to allow the CAS to investigate these new plans.

[
28
]

In the late fall, Ms. St. Hill informed the parents that the CAS
would apprehend the new baby at birth. The parents were encouraged to complete
the parenting programs.

[
29
]

The new child, Richard B., Jr., was born on November 11, 2007. R.B.
was present for the birth. Following discharge from the hospital, F.H., feared that
CAS would apprehend Robert Jr., and went into hiding with the baby at her
aunt’s residence.  R.B. remained at his mother’s residence, but had frequent
contact with F.H.

[
30
]

On December 20, 2007, R.B. went to a Toronto police station to make a complaint about F.H., suggesting that she
had caused some damage to his car. The officer who took the complaint, Calvin
Clark, testified that R.B. was initially evasive in providing information.  It was
later explained in R.B.’s testimony that his hesitation to provide information
was a result of his fear that the CAS would be called.

[
31
]

Richard Jr. was apprehended from the mother on December 23, 2007 by
the Metro CAS acting on information received from the Durham CAS. The
Protection Application sought temporary custody of this child, with the
proceedings to be transferred to Durham. The Durham CAS brought an Amended Protection Application with a
first court date of April 25, 2007 seeking Crown wardship with no access for
the purposes of adoption.

[
32
]

In this Amended Application the CAS neglected to indicate which
section of the
CFSA
was being used to seek a finding that the child was
in need of protection. This issue was raised by the court at trial at the end
of the father’s case and before the start of the mother’s case. It appeared
that neither counsel nor either party were aware of this oversight. The court
granted a motion to amend the pleadings pursuant to
rule 26.01
of the
Rules
of Civil Procedure, R.R.O. 1990 Reg. 194
:

26.01  On
motion at any stage of an action the court shall grant leave to amend a
pleading on such terms as are just, unless prejudice would result that could
not be compensated for by costs or an adjournment.

[
33
]

The amendment allowed the CAS to seek a finding that Richard Jr. was
a child in need of protection under the same sections as were pleaded in
relation to his siblings,
ss. 37(2)
(a)(i), 37(2)(b)(i), 37(2)(b)(ii), and
37(2)(g) of the
CFSA
.

[
34
]

Neither party was prejudiced by the amendment. All parties
recognized that the issues before the court were whether a finding should be
made that Richard Jr. was a child in need of protection – which was ultimately
consented to – and whether the children should be returned to the parents or
made Crown wards. As the father’s case was just finished, he was given the
opportunity to reopen the case, but declined. It appeared that mother was going
to be the only witness for her case.

Current Matters

[
35
]

On January 8, 2008 father indicated to Ms. Hill that the parents’
goal was to reunite and have the children returned to their care; however, less
than a week later the mother indicted that she had obtained a new apartment
without the father, recognizing that their relationship was going nowhere.

[
36
]

The undated Kinship Report was completed by the CAS.  The report
indicates that the maternal grandmother abandoned her plan prior to an
investigation.

[
37
]

The paternal grandmother was cooperative during the assessment
process; however, she missed appointments, failed to have her references
completed and failed to obtain the CPIC checks on her sons, who frequented her
residence. She was unable to provide a permanent plan. She had just moved into
a new residence, but indicated that she would soon be moving again. The report
indicates that she felt that the parents “would work things out and would soon
have children returned to their care.”

[
38
]

It would be unfair to the children to be raised without a constant
caregiver and with the threat that they may be moved at some indefinite time in
the future. The report concludes by not recommending placement of the children
with their paternal grandmother. Neither she nor either parent has taken steps
to challenge the report.

[
39
]

On March 11, 2008 Ms. Hill met with the parents. Again she gave the
parents a copy of the Plan of Care and read the expectations that the CAS expected
to be fulfilled prior to returning the children – counselling and drug testing
– and gave the parents the names and phone numbers of agencies that could
provide these services. It appears that letters dated March 13, 2007; March 30,
2007; May 8, 2007; May 14, 2007; December 28, 2007; October 1, 2008; October 3,
2008 and October 14, 2008 from the CAS to one or both parents, set out the
expectations of the CAS for drug testing and counselling.

[
40
]

On April 15, 2008 the parents became involved in a physical
altercation in the lobby of the CAS office where they had attended for their
supervised access. The parties had broken up again and the dispute was over
whether a ring that father had given mother should be returned to him. It
appears, from the testimony of the receptionist who witnessed the altercation,
that the mother was the aggressor. The police were called. As a result of this
incident, the CAS directed the parents to exercise access individually, rather
than as a couple.

[
41
]

To his credit, R.B. attended the PARS program in 2008, even though
he felt that he did not need the assistance. Leanne Trafagander, a family
counsellor who works in this program, testified as to R.B.’s participation. The
goal of the program is to teach alternative behaviours to abusing men and to
give them insight into their abuse.  R.B. continued to deny any abusive
behaviour. While he was in one session, F.H. attended the PARS office
indicating that he was forcing her to remain in the car while he was in the
sessions. She was crying, shaking and agitated. She expressed her fear of him
and a desire to end the relationship.

[
42
]

The conclusion of the two facilitators of the PARS program, Ms.
Trafagander and Todd Acres, is set out in their report which was filed as
Exhibit 6:

[R.B.] acknowledged very minimal abuse against
his partner. He denied ever having used physical force or any past police
involvement, which is contrary to the information supplied by the referral
source. There is reason to believe that [R.B.] has continued to be abusive and
controlling towards his partner.

[
43
]

Ms. Trafagander indicated that R.B. did not pass the program. While
the CAS had considered placing the children with R.B., his failure to pass the
PARS program, the continued domestic violence and the failure on his part to
undergo drug testing led the CAS to abandon this plan.

[
44
]

In October, despite the fact that the two older children had been in
foster care for more than twice the allowable time limit, the CAS sought yet another
adjournment of the trial. This appears to have been done in part to give the
parents another chance to meet CAS and court expectations, such that the
children might be returned to their care.

[
45
]

In the next month, November 2008, a neighbour living across a
courtyard from the parents witnessed R.B. assaulting F.H. The neighbour called
the police. When the police arrived, the parents were gone. Detective Marshall
has testified that F.H., in giving her statement, gave the same story as
related by the neighbour – that R.B. pushed, grabbed and strangled F.H.,
leaving her with blood on her face.  R.B. suggests that he “grabbed her hand
for a second.”  If R.B.’s version is correct, it is surprising that a neighbour
witnessing the incident would phone the police and that her story was the same
as that related by F.H. to the police.

[
46
]

R.B. was arrested December 9, 2008 and released on bail on December
11, 2008, with conditions, including a no contact order with F.H. One week
later, despite the no contact order,  there was another confrontation between
the two. He was charged with breach of his bail conditions and detained. On
February 20, 2009 he pled guilty to the November, 2008 assault and was
sentenced to time served, plus a probation order again prohibiting contact with
F.H. In subsequent testimony, both parents have indicated that they resumed
sexual relations by the end of February 2009, despite the court order of the
previous week prohibiting contact.  By mid-March she was pregnant again with
her fourth child by R.B.

[
47
]

For parents who voice a commitment to their children, the
expectations of the CAS seemed minimal; however, both parents have failed to
carry through with expectations.  R.B. has had three years to complete drug
screens following the positive test for cocaine. He has failed and considered
it harassment when reminded to do so.

[
48
]

Both parents have failed to complete counselling, despite frequently
indicating a willingness to do so. By their own estimate they have had ten to
twenty separations. Both parents have ignored court orders to stay away from
one another and have persisted in a pattern of an on-again off-again
relationship, marked by allegations of domestic violence that have resulted in
frequent intervention by the police.

[
49
]

Each of Alizeah and Anthony was found to be a child in need of
protection on November 20, 2006. Prior to the testimony of the adoption worker,
counsel indicated that the parties consented to a finding that Richard Jr. was
a child in need of protection pursuant to
s. 37(2)
(l) of the
CFSA
, but
as this was not the section used when the amendment was made earlier in the
trial, the consent was not accepted by the court.

[
50
]

While they have had little opportunity to parent Richard Jr., the
parents, through their ongoing physical and verbal confrontations, often
resulting in police intervention and criminal charges, pose a risk that the
children will be physically harmed during the disputes or emotionally harmed by
witnessing such violence between their parents.

[
51
]

The parents have shown minimal effort to address the issues that
caused the CAS intervention and led to the original finding.  As such, Richard Jr.
is found to be a child in need of protection pursuant to
s. 37(2)
(b) and
37(2)(g) of the
CFSA
:

37(2)  A child is in need of protection where,

….

(b)  there is a risk that the child is likely to suffer physical
harm inflicted by the person having charge of the child or caused by or
resulting from that person’s,

(i)  failure to adequately care for, provide for, supervise or
protect the child, or

(ii)  pattern of neglect in caring for, providing for, supervising
or protecting the child.

….

(g)
there is a risk that the child is likely to suffer emotional harm of the kind
described in subclause (f) (i), (ii), (iii), (iv) or (v) resulting from the actions,
failure to act or pattern of neglect on the part of the child’s parent or the
person having charge of the child;

DISPOSITION

[
52
]

The disposition is to be made in the best interests of the children
following a consideration of the factors listed in
s. 37(3)
of the
CFSA
.
Several of these factors appear to be of greater importance in this case:

37(3)  Where a person is directed in this Part
to make an order or determination in the best interests of a child, the person
shall take into consideration those of the following circumstances of the case
that he or she considers relevant:

1.   The child’s physical, mental and emotional
needs, and the appropriate care or treatment to meet those needs.

2.   The child’s physical, mental and emotional
level of development.

3.   The child’s cultural background.

….

5.   The importance for the child’s development
of a positive relationship with a parent and a secure place as a member of a
family.

6.   The child’s relationships and emotional
ties to a parent, sibling, relative, other member of the child’s extended
family or member of the child’s community.

….

8.   The merits of a plan for the child’s care
proposed by a society, including a proposal that the child be placed for
adoption or adopted, compared with the merits of the child remaining with or
returning to a parent.

….

10.  The effects on the child of delay in the
disposition of the case.

11.  The risk that the child may suffer harm
through being removed from, kept away from, returned to or allowed to remain in
the care of a parent.

12.  The degree of risk, if any, that justified
the finding that the child is in need of protection.

….

[
53
]

Due to the length of time that the children have been in care, the
court has only two options: return of the children to one or both of the
parents, or Crown wardship as proposed by the CAS such that the children can be
adopted.

A) Parents’ Plans

[
54
]

In his Plan of Care filed both in January and May 2007, R.B.
expressed the intent to remain resident with his mother in a four bedroom
house. It appears that he and his mother have moved, as in his testimony he
indicated that they now live in a two bedroom townhouse. He also reveals in his
testimony that he will move from his mother’s residence as soon as possible and
find a place suitable for the children, although he has no idea how long that
will take. He told Ms. St. Hill in September, 2006 that he would find his own
accommodations, but is still dependent upon his mother for housing.

[
55
]

In this same Plan of Care, presented at trial but prepared two years
earlier, he indicates that F.H. is an immature and irresponsible parent who is
incapable of caring for the children. In his testimony, while indicating a
desire to find housing for himself and the children, he also indicates a desire
to reunite with F.H. as soon as the children are returned, thinking that all of
their problems would then disappear. His plan would put the children on hold
until he finds accommodations, but those accommodations may only be temporary
if he then wishes to reunite with F.H.

[
56
]

In the same Plan of Care he indicates that he will return to school
in September, 2007. Why wait so long when he could have enrolled in classes in
January 2007? In fact, the only school credits that he received from the time
he presented the Plan of Care to trial in 2009 were those received while he was
in jail.

[
57
]

He indicates that he will have the support of his family, both
financially and in child care, and yet no family member attended any day of
this hearing, as he stated that they are “extremely busy”. He indicates that he
will send each child to private school and yet he has had only sporadic
employment, three months in 2007 and 2008, and does not appear to have any
specific job skills. I question whether he is being realistic.

[
58
]

In her Plan of Care filed in June 2007, F.H. indicates that she
resides with her mother and sister and that they plan to find larger
accommodations to provide for the children.  F.H. has moved several times since
filing the Plan of Care and presently resides on her own.

[
59
]

She indicates that she intends to take counselling, but she has
never completed a counselling program although she has reached the intake stage
on several occasions. She indicates that her relationship with R.B. is over and
she has no intention of having a relationship with him, yet they have continued
to have an on-again off-again relationship that resulted in several emergency
calls to the police.

[
60
]

F.H. appears to be socially isolated, testifying that she has no
friends, perhaps a reason she has been so dependent on R.B. She recited a
litany of abuse from R.B. and indicated that she understood the cycle of abuse
in which women return to abusing partners. Despite this apparent understanding,
towards the end of her testimony she expressed the hope that they would
reunite, expressing her love for him.

[
61
]

Neither parent has put forward a definite plan for these children in
the future. Both have indicated that they will find new accommodations, but
such plans are indefinite. How much longer will the children have to wait?
There is still uncertainty as to whether these parents will reunite. Both seem
to be expressing a desire to do so despite their inability to live violence-free
in the past.

[
62
]

While both express the full support of their respective families,
not one family member has presented evidence in support of returning the children
to the care of one or both of the parents. No family member even appeared at
court in support of either parent. Each parent testified as to the potential
monetary gifts from their respective mothers as the result of pending lawsuits,
but no details or confirmation from either mother has been presented. No one
has testified on behalf of either parent, other than themselves.

[
63
]

Both parents failed to follow the order of Justice Gunsolus of
October 7, 2008 to seek counselling and for R.B. to provide drug testing. There
were a number of documented instances of the parents seeing one another despite
court orders that they have no communication.

[
64
]

There has been no evidence that the parents ever physically hurt the
children.  However, they fail to recognize the impact of domestic violence upon
children. The Family Services supervisor, Paulette Letang and the Children’s Services
worker, Karen Saunders, outlined some of the potential effects of domestic
violence on children – repetition of the behaviour when they become adults, low
self esteem, fear, conflict with the law, bed wetting, violent social
interactions as children, poor school performance, anger and anxiety.

[
65
]

The impact of domestic violence upon children has frequently been
reviewed in Ontario courts. In
Children’s
Aid Society of Toronto v. S.A.C.
,
2005 ONCJ 274 (CanLII)
, [2005] O.J. No. 2154 (O.C.J.) , aff’d

2005 CanLII 43289 (ON SC)
, [2005] O.J. No. 4718 (S.C.), aff’d
2007 ONCA 474
, leave to appeal to S.C.C.
refused [2007] S.C.C.A. No. 462, Zuker J. at trial stated at paras. 131 and
144:

Evidence of
family violence is relevant in so far as it assists the court in determining
what orders will best promote the interests of the children. The court will
have regard to the fact that family violence may be directly or indirectly
relevant to a child’s welfare in a variety of ways and may be relevant even
where it is not directed at or witnessed by the children.

…

Research
has shown that domestic violence places children at risk of harm on a number of
levels. First, the domestic violence perpetrator may also be directly,
physically or sexually abusive to the child. Second, witnessing violence
perpetrated against their mother may have an abusive and detrimental impact on
a child’s development. Children can develop an inappropriate maturity and sense
of responsibility that can inhibit their ability to develop it an  appropriate level.
Third, a perpetrator may abuse a child as part of the violence against their
partner. Fourth, children can feel guilty, blame themselves and feel depressed.
Fifth, children can develop fears, insecurity and low self-esteem as a result
of witnessing domestic violence. Finally, children can suffer emotional
confusion that can result in bedwetting, nightmares, sleeping or eating
disturbances, self-harm and weight loss. I have absolutely no doubt that this
child is likely to suffer significant harm unless I make the order that the
society is seeking.

[
66
]

In
Jewish Family and Child Service v. R.K.
,
[2008] O.J. No.
1940
. (O.C.J.), Sherr J. commented upon the impact of domestic violence on
children at para 28:

Domestic violence places children at
risk on a number of levels. Witnessing violence perpetrated against their
mother may have an abusive and detrimental impact on a child’s development.
Children may feel guilty, blame themselves and feel depressed. They can develop
fears, insecurity and low self-esteem as a result of witnessing domestic
violence. They can suffer emotional confusion that can result in bedwetting,
nightmares, sleeping or eating disturbances, self-harm and weight loss.

[
67
]

For the past three years these children have been shielded form the
ongoing conflict of their parents as the children have been in foster care. While
with the children on supervised access visits, it appears that they may have
the relationship of a caring aunt or uncle demonstrating a positive interaction
for short periods of time; however, they have been unwilling or unable to take
the responsibility needed for parenting and the obligations that go with it.

[
68
]

They express their love for their children and yet F.H. and R.B. have
been unable, during the three years that this case has been ongoing, to avoid
conflict resulting in police intervention. They have frequently breached court
orders to stay away from each other. Both express good intentions, but neither
parent has been able to follow through.

[
69
]

The CAS would have considered returning the children to R.B. if drug
screens showed no drugs and if he stayed away from mother. During his testimony
he indicated that he had recently taken some drug testing, but when the court
resumed more than a month after this testimony, no drug results were presented.

[
70
]

R.B. seems to be overly dependent upon his mother, expecting that
even though she is single, she will continue to financially support him. He is
the father of not only these three children, but the father of a child yet to
be born and the father of a child from another woman.  He seems quick to blame
others for his problems, taking no responsibility himself. He will turn
twenty-seven this year and still lives with his mother. He has had sporadic
employment and has not followed through with his intentions to pursue his
education. Despite being a person with time to spare, he has failed to find
time to give the CAS the results of a drug test in the past three years or to
take counselling.

B) CAS Plan

[
71
]

The CAS plan for the children is adoption. Testimony was given by a CAS
adoption worker, Jane Rees, that each of these children is a suitable candidate
for adoption as they have no special needs. She expressed confidence that the
children could be placed together, within three to six months, in an adoptive
home that recognizes the cultural heritage of these children. Her confidence
was expressed even though, in her six years with the adoption department, she
indicated that she had only been involved with one case in which more than one
child was placed for adoption in the same home.

[
72
]

The CAS has sixty families approved for adoptions.  Ms. Rees
indicated that she had three adoptive families in mind that had a related
cultural background to these three children. These families have yet to be
approached about these children and their willingness to take more than one
child.

[
73
]

The adoption department apparently recognizes the need for the
children to be placed together and to be in a placement that recognizes their
cultural heritage. The same cannot be said for the department that places
children in foster care. While the two older children have been placed together
in a home that has seen other foster children come and go, Richard Jr. has
never been with his siblings even though he has been in foster care for
nineteen months, almost his entire life. He has been restricted to seeing his
siblings only during the short weekly access visits granted to the parents.

[
74
]

Due to the desire to keep the children together and to find an
adoptive family of similar cultural heritage, the CAS may have to look outside
of their own region for a suitable family. Is her timetable of placement within
three to six months realistic if they have to look outside of Durham?

[
75
]

If the CAS has sixty approved families for adoption, as stated by Ms.
Rees, why is the CAS not prepared to immediately place the children in an
adoptive home without further delay? If none of these families is viable for
these children, why has the CAS not done some initial exploration outside of
the region already? The only reason given seems to be the potential heartbreak
for the adoptive family if the children are not made available for adoption. At
a minimum, they could have one family in mind which would be approached
immediately upon the children being available for adoption. The CAS must
remember that the paramount purpose of the legislation as outlined in
s. 1
of
the
CFSA
is the best interests, protection and well being of children,
not the chance of disappointing prospective adoptive parents:

1(1)  The paramount purpose of this Act is to
promote the best interests, protection and well being of children.

[
76
]

The
Family Law Rules
, R.R.O. 2008, Reg. 151 set out time
guidelines to bring Protection Applications to a conclusion:

33(1)  Every child protection case, including a
status review application is governed by the following timetable:

Step in the case

Maximum time for completion from
start of case

First hearing, if child has been
apprehended

5 days

Service and filing of answers and
plans of care

30 days

Temporary care and custody hearing

35 days

Settlement conference

80 days

Hearing

120 days

[
77
]

These guidelines may be difficult to achieve due to the number of
steps to be taken in a child welfare case: the first court attendance within
five days of the apprehension of the child, the processing of the Legal Aid
Applications, finding and making an appointment with counsel, preparation and
service of pleadings, preparation of Reply materials by the CAS, setting aside
sufficient court time for a contested temporary care hearing, settlement
conference and trial management conference. In addition, the CAS is expected to
work with the family to remedy the situation that caused the apprehension.

[
78
]

The
CFSA
has put time limits on the amount of time that
children can remain in the care of the CAS.

52  Where an application is made under
subsection 40(1) or a matter is brought before the court to determine whether a
child is in need of protection and the determination has not been made within
three months after the commencement of the proceeding, the court,

(a)
shall by order fix a date for the hearing of the application,

….

70(1)  Subject to subsections (3) and (4), the
court shall not make an order for society wardship under this Part that results
in a child being a society ward for a period exceeding,

(a)  12
months, if the child is less than 6 years of age on the day the

court
makes an order for society wardship, or

(2)
In calculating the period referred to in subsection (1), time during which a
child has been in a society’s care and custody under,

…

(b)  a temporary order made under clause 51 (2)
(d), shall be counted.

[
79
]

The planning for the lives of these children has been placed on hold
for over three years while they waited for their parents to sort out their
relationship. Both the parents and the CAS have delayed the implementation of a
stable plan for the children. These children need stability; they children can
wait no longer. The court adopts the words of Karswick J. in
Children’s Aid
Society of the Region of Peel vs. A.O.

2006 ONCJ 149 (CanLII)
, [2006] O.J. No. 1779, at para.
111
,
in commenting on the time limitations in child welfare cases:

The statutory
limitation has been enacted for a valid purpose, which is to serve the best
interest of the children so that they do not remain in a legal state of
uncertainty and instability. Children have a right to have their present living
and future decided in a timely manner so that short-term attachments are not
repeatedly severed. Their lives cannot be unduly subject to disruptions and
uncertainty. The provision laudably addresses the very desirable objective of
making decisions in a reasonably timely manner.

[
80
]

All participants must share the blame for these unjust delays in
child welfare proceedings. Time limits have been legislated by 1999 amendments
to the
CFSA
in recognition of the need to make a stable permanent plan
for children. The same amendments deleted provision
s. 57(6)
, which provided
that the court should not make an order for Crown wardship unless satisfied that
the circumstances justifying the order were unlikely to change within a
reasonably foreseeable time not to exceed twenty-four months

[
81
]

Surprisingly, in October 2008, after the case had been set for trial
and after the children had been in foster care for over two years in
contravention of the time directions in the
Family Law Rule
s and the
CFSA
,
the CAS sought a seven month adjournment for the trial. As a result, Alizeah
and Anthony had been in care for almost three years by the time the case
reached the trial stage. Richard Jr. had been in care for eighteen months,
almost his entire life, and there had not even been a finding that this child
was in need of protection as defined under the
CFSA
.

[
82
]

The Durham CAS initiated these proceedings, but has failed to act in
the best interests of these children by apparently ignoring the time guidelines
set out in child welfare legislation. The delays in this case are inexcusable
and have occurred to the detriment of these children. The Durham CAS should
review their practises to prevent such delays in the future.

[
83
]

The parents have also delayed these proceedings by their inability
or unwillingness to address the issues that brought the case to court. The CAS
gave them too much time to plan for the children. Even during the trial, each
of the parents caused delay. Twice the mother had to leave as she was sick,
likely due to the pregnancy that occurred at a time the two parents were under
court order to stay away from one another. Two-and-a-half days were lost as the
father, without forewarning to counsel or to the court, left court. It turned
out that he was arrested later that day and detained for two nights. These
delays raised scheduling issues that caused a further delay of two months.

[
84
]

In considering the factors of best interests as outlined in
s. 37(3)

of the
CFSA
, only the important factors of relationship by blood and
cultural background favour the parents. The parents, by their lack of progress
in the past three years, leave the court with no option as they have failed to
present a viable plan. Neither parent has suitable accommodation for the
children, only an intention to find it. This lack of housing, despite over
three years to plan for the return of the children, in itself defeats the
parents’ plan.

[
85
]

However, even if the parents did have adequate housing to provide
for their children, they have not resolved their ongoing domestic violence. The
parents have continued to have frequent conflict, resulting in ten to twenty
separations and requiring police intervention, despite CAS and court directives
to have no contact. The same conditions exist today that justified the November
20, 2006 order of Justice Eberhard in finding that the children are in need of
protection. Both parents are uncertain as to their future relationship. They
verbally acknowledge a need for couples counselling, but have failed to receive
same although given three years to complete it.

[
86
]

The permanency planning for these children has been delayed beyond
the statutory guidelines. They must be removed from their temporary placements.
Due to their young ages and lack of special needs, each of the children is a
good candidate for adoption to find a secure place as a member of a family. The
CAS is confident that an adoptive home recognizing the children’s cultural
heritage can be found.

[
87
]

The parents, through their attendance at the majority of access
visits and their attendance during the hearing, have shown some commitment to
these children. In the event that the children have not been placed for
adoption within the three to six month period proposed by the CAS, the parents
may be entitled to bring a Status Review Application pursuant to s. 65.1 of the
Act.

[
88
]

Without being informed that the children have in fact been placed
for adoption, the parents would not have the opportunity to exercise this

[
89
]

ADDITIONAL MATTERS

[
90
]

Another child is due to be born near the beginning of November 2009 to
this couple. If the parents wish to parent this child, they should immediately
direct their minds to presenting a viable plan. They need to be able to
implement a specific plan, rather than present vague intentions. Their plans
should make reference to their ongoing relationship with each other and with
their families, counselling, drug testing, housing, finances, primary care and
access.

[
91
]

The CAS should ensure that, if they become involved with this new
child, unnecessary delays are avoided. While some may question appointing
counsel for babies, a legal representative for a newborn may advocate to the
